title: Azure VMs: Finding, Inspecting, and Stopping (Properly)
intro: Azure Virtual Machines are the equivalent of EC2 instances. The CLI patterns carry over, but there's one Azure-specific trap that costs companies real money: a VM that's 'stopped' is still billed unless it's 'deallocated'.

steps.prompt: List VMs in all groups, with their power state and public IPs (the -d flag adds those details), as a table.
steps.fake_output:
Name        ResourceGroup  PowerState      PublicIps     Location
----------  -------------  --------------  ------------  ----------
vm-web-01   rg-web-prod    VM running      20.61.14.8    westeurope
vm-web-02   rg-web-prod    VM running      20.61.14.9    westeurope
vm-batch-01 rg-data-prod   VM stopped                    westeurope
steps.explanation: Two web VMs are running; vm-batch-01 is 'stopped'.
steps.why: Without -d (--show-details) the list has no power state or IPs, because it needs extra API calls per VM. 'VM stopped' is the important word here: see the next steps.

steps.prompt: Check vm-batch-01's detailed status in rg-data-prod.
expected_commands: az vm get-instance-view --resource-group rg-data-prod --name vm-batch-01 --query instanceView.statuses
az vm get-instance-view -g rg-data-prod -n vm-batch-01 --query instanceView.statuses
steps.explanation: PowerState/stopped: the OS is shut down, but the VM still holds its compute allocation.
steps.why: Stopping from inside the OS ('sudo shutdown') or with 'az vm stop' leaves the VM allocated on a host, and you keep paying for its compute. Only PowerState/deallocated stops compute billing.

steps.prompt: Deallocate vm-batch-01 in rg-data-prod so it stops costing compute.
steps.explanation: The compute allocation is released; you now pay only for its disks.
steps.why: The trade-off: a deallocated VM loses its dynamic public IP (it may get a different one on start) and its temporary disk. If anything depends on the IP, make it static first. azure-incident-004 is exactly that failure.

steps.prompt: See which VM sizes are available in westeurope, to plan a resize.
steps.fake_output:
Name              NumberOfCores  MemoryInMb
----------------  -------------  ----------
Standard_B2s      2              4096
Standard_D4s_v5   4              16384
Standard_E8s_v5   8              65536
...
steps.explanation: B-series is burstable and cheap, D is general purpose, E is memory-optimised.
steps.why: Size families map to workloads, the same idea as AWS's t/m/r families. B-series 'burstable' VMs run out of CPU credits under sustained load and get throttled, which is a common cause of mysteriously slow servers.

steps.prompt: Resize vm-web-02 in rg-web-prod to Standard_D4s_v5.
expected_commands: az vm resize --resource-group rg-web-prod --name vm-web-02 --size Standard_D4s_v5
az vm resize -g rg-web-prod -n vm-web-02 --size Standard_D4s_v5
steps.fake_output: (the VM restarts on the new size; about 2 minutes)
steps.why: A resize restarts the VM, so do one instance at a time behind a load balancer. If the new size isn't available on the current hardware cluster, you must deallocate first. For fleets, use a VM Scale Set and roll out a new model instead of resizing by hand.
